entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Victor of Capua was a sixth-century bishop of Capua in Italy, playing a pivotal role in the early Christianization of southern Italy.

As the Bishop of Capua, Victor of Capua worked to spread Christianity throughout his diocese, establishing monasteries and churches that would serve as centers of learning and spiritual growth. His efforts helped to establish Christianity as a major force in southern Italy, paving the way for the region's eventual integration into the Byzantine Empire.

Victor of Capua's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, influencing the development of Christian theology and practice in the region. His writings on monasticism and spirituality continue to be studied by scholars today.

The significance of Victor of Capua lies in his role as a key figure in the early Christianization of southern Italy, shaping the spiritual landscape of the region for centuries to come.

"thumbnailUrl": "", "quote": "", "legacySummary": "", "summary": "Victor of Capua (died 554 CE) was a 6th-century Italian bishop and biblical scholar — Bishop of Capua in Campania — who is primarily known for a significant contribution to biblical textual history: he is associated with the 'Fuldensis Gospel Harmony', a Latin revision of Tatian's Diatessaron (the famous 2nd-century Gospel harmony compiled by the Syriac Christian scholar Tatian) that Victor commissioned or composed. The Codex Fuldensis — a 6th-century Latin New Testament manuscript housed at the Abbey of Fulda (from which it takes its name) — includes a Latin version of a Gospel harmony that Victor prepared in 545 CE, with a preface explaining his editorial work: he noted that he had discovered a Latin Diatessaron that had been poorly rendered and had revised and reorganised it to align with the canonical four-gospel structure.

Victor's Gospel harmony is significant for several reasons in biblical scholarship: it preserves elements of an ancient Gospel harmony tradition (Tatian's Diatessaron was one of the most widely used Christian texts before the four-gospel canon was fully established, especially in Syriac and Eastern Christianity), it demonstrates the continued interest in Gospel harmonisation in Western Christianity three centuries after Tatian, and it is evidence for the circulation of Diatessaron-related materials in Latin Christianity that had largely moved away from harmonisation toward the canonical four-gospel text.

Victor's scholarly activity places him in the tradition of 6th-century Italian ecclesiastical scholars — the generation that included Cassiodorus, Boethius, and Pope Gregory the Great — who worked to preserve, revise, and transmit the texts of the Christian tradition during the turbulent period of Ostrogothic rule and the Byzantine reconquest.
